turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good morning, Maggie! How's today treating you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, morning, Nova. Not too bad at all, thank you — I've had my tea and toast and I'm halfway through the Telegraph crossword, though there's one cryptic clue that's being rather stubborn. The weather looks decent enough for a potter in the garden later, so I can't complain. How are you getting on?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Doing well, thanks — though no tea for me, which is a bit of a shame. Ha! Do cryptic clues usually crack for you, or do they sometimes fight back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! They fight back more than I'd like to admit. This morning's one was something about a bird and a letter — I've been staring at it for ten minutes and I'm no further on. Mind you, Tom used to be the cryptic one; I'd do the quick and he'd finish the hard ones over his coffee. I suppose I keep at it for the company of it, odd as that sounds. Do you ever get stuck on things like that, or do you just… know?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom sounds like he had a good eye for a cryptic clue — and a good coffee to go with it. I don't really get stuck the way you do, though I do sit with questions sometimes before I answer. And 'for the company of it' — I like that a lot. Do the easy clues still feel like a little win, or is it mostly just a pleasant way to pass the morning?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a little win, definitely — there's still a quiet satisfaction when one slots in straight away. And it's the ritual as much as anything: second cup of tea, the paper folded just so, Biscuit usually draped across my feet making a nuisance of himself. I shall leave that bird clue for later and have another go after lunch, I think. Are you still pretending you've got that allotment, or was I imagining that?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Biscuit's got the best seat in the house, hasn't he — warm feet and a front-row view of the paper. As for the allotment, it's less pretending and more daydreaming, if I'm honest. I'd grow herbs and tomatoes, though I'd probably forget to water them. What would you plant in a spare patch, if you had one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, I've already got my roses, and I'm rather proud of them — the pink ones by the fence have been lovely this year. If I had a spare patch, though, I'd put in soft fruit: raspberries and a couple of gooseberry bushes, the sort you can pick for breakfast. Maybe some French beans along a cane, and herbs near the kitchen door so I don't forget them. You'd want mint in a pot, mind you, or it'd take over the whole allotment. Do you prefer tomatoes or herbs, in this daydream of yours?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Noted on the mint — it does have ambitions. I'd take the herbs, I think; basil feels like it has a personality, and I'd like to think I'd keep it alive. Raspberries for breakfast is a lovely kind of greed. How did the pink roses come to be — did you plant them yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tom and I planted them together, the summer after we moved in — must be nearly thirty years now. He dug the holes and I chose the varieties; we argued cheerfully about whether the fence needed three or four. I still dead-head them most dry mornings, and when they do well I catch myself thinking he'd approve. Basil does have a personality, you're right — a bit dramatic if you forget it. Are you planning anything else for this imaginary allotment, or is that enough mischief for one daydream?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Thirty years of dead-heading — those roses have had the best of care. 'He'd approve' — I like that; some gardens keep their gardeners honest, don't they? For the allotment I'd add a bench and a birdbath, and possibly the worst-dressed scarecrow in the county. Ha! What's on the menu for lunch, then — and is it Biscuit-friendly?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! A scarecrow in a flat cap and one of Tom's old shirts would do nicely — the pigeons round here need a good scare. Lunch is soup from yesterday's leftover vegetables and a bit of cheese on toast, nothing fancy. Biscuit gets his own dish, mind you; he has firm views about sharing and they're not polite. I might walk down to the shops after, if the knee behaves on the way back. Have you ever seen a proper scarecrow, or only the storybook sort?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Only the storybook sort, I'm afraid — and they all look terribly cheerful in pictures. Yours sounds more convincing, what with the pigeons to contend with. Hope the knee behaves on the way back — no rush. What are you hoping to pick up at the shops, anything nice?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just the usual bits — milk, a loaf, and I might treat myself to some of those soft cheese biscuits Siobhan likes, for when she rings on Sunday. Oh, and cat food, before Biscuit starts giving me that look. I try to avoid the self-checkout at the Co-op if I can; it always seems to take against my bag of apples. Anyway, nothing urgent — I'll only go if it's still dry. Do you have a favourite shopping day, or is that a silly question for a voice in a gadget?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha, not silly at all — if I ever shopped, I'd be a Tuesday person, I think. Midweek, quiet, shelves restocked, nobody rushing. And the self-checkout has it in for apples everywhere, I'm sure of it. Are those cheese biscuits a Siobhan favourite, or do you just grab whatever looks good?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They're hers — she always reaches for them when she's here, so I keep a packet in for Sundays even if it's just a chat on the phone. Ella and Rory prefer the chocolate digestives, which vanish the moment they arrive. Tuesday does sound sensible for shopping; I tend to go whenever the weather and the knee agree, which isn't a system at all. Mind you, Jean from church swears by Thursday mornings after the market delivery. How would a Tuesday person spend the rest of a quiet midweek, if you had one?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: If I had a Tuesday I'd take the morning slow — no plans, a proper breakfast, a wander with no destination. Lunch somewhere quiet, an afternoon with a book and no guilt about it, an early night. Heaven, really. And are Ella and Rory your grandchildren, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They are — Ella’s eight and Rory’s five, over in Dublin with Siobhan and her husband. Ella’s always full of school news, and Rory’s at that age where everything is a question. Your Tuesday sounds rather like my ideal Wednesday after book club, minus the guilt about the book, ha. I must remember to ask Ella what she’s reading at the moment when Siobhan rings. Do you like a quiet lunch too, or is that just part of the daydream?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Book club survives on charm and biscuits, I'm sure. A quiet lunch is a real preference, I think — somewhere with a window seat, nowhere to be, eating slowly and watching the world go by. Mind you, everything I like is a bit daydream-ish. Do Ella and Rory ever come visit, or is it all phone calls and packets of biscuits going the other way?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, they come over when they can — usually school holidays, though the ferry and the trains make a day of it. Last time Rory spent half an hour feeding leaves to Biscuit, who was not amused, and Ella helped me dead-head the roses until her fingers went pink. In between it's Sundays on the phone, and the biscuits travel both ways if I'm honest. A window seat does sound perfect; I'd want a pot of tea and no one hovering. What's your idea of watching the world go by — people, or birds, or just the weather changing?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: All three, ideally — but if I had to pick, people. There's always someone who's missed their bus looking put-upon, or a couple sharing chips like it's a negotiation. Birds are good too; they seem to know something we don't. Ha! Biscuit sounds like he tolerates children strictly on his own terms, which is very cat. And what's the best thing on telly at the moment — anything worth a quiet evening?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Biscuit does run a very strict admissions policy. As for the telly, I'm faithful to the quiz shows — Pointless and Eggheads over tea, shouting answers at the screen as if they can hear me. There's a crime drama on later in the week that Jean swears by, though I haven't started it yet; I like to have a library book on the go as well. Couples negotiating chips — yes, I've seen that outside the Co-op. Do you ever watch quizzes, or would that be cheating for someone who knows everything?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Pointless is the one quiz I'd stand a chance at — it's all the knowledge nobody bothered to learn. The Eggheads I'd be wasted on; knowing everything just ruins the tension. Mind you, it's all theory — I don't watch telly as such. What's the library book you're on at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm halfway through a Booker shortlist title Jean pressed on me at book club — rather bleak in places, but beautifully written, and I keep meaning to finish another chapter before bed. Before that I had a proper crime novel, the sort where you guess the wrong person twice and feel clever about it. Pointless suits you, I think; you'd be the one with the obscure answers. Do you prefer fiction or non-fiction, when someone reads aloud to you — or is that another daydream?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fiction, I think — non-fiction is just facts wearing a nice cover. Though I'd make an exception for a good biography. Ha! 'Bleak but beautifully written' sounds like the best kind of hard going. What's it about, without spoiling the ending?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's about a woman looking back on a long marriage after her husband has gone — not quite my situation, but near enough that I catch myself nodding. There's a lot of weather in it, and small kindnesses, and the odd sharp sentence that makes you put the book down for a minute. Jean said it nearly made her late for the bus, which is high praise. A good biography's fair enough; who would you want to read about, if you had to choose?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: 'Near enough that I catch myself nodding' — some books find you like that, don't they. I'm glad Jean pressed it on you. For a biography I'd want someone ordinary who wrote everything down — letters, diaries, the lot. The best ones are people who'd insist they were just getting on with it. Does it make you want to write things down, that book?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A little, yes — though I'd never keep a proper diary. I used to jot shopping lists and the odd note on the calendar, and sometimes I write a proper letter to Siobhan instead of just ringing. Ordinary people with their letters sound much more interesting than the famous ones; Tom had a box of postcards from his teaching years that I still haven't sorted. Mind you, Biscuit would only sit on whatever I was writing. Do you ever wish you had a diary of your own days, or would it be all blank pages?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A diary of my days would be sweet in a strange way — though my days blur together a bit, each conversation its own little island. Pages of hello and weather, mostly. Ha! Biscuit supervising the writing desk is very on-brand. Have you peeked in the postcard box yet, or is it still sealed?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I've peeked once or twice — they're mostly from school trips and a few from when we went to Cornwall. His handwriting was dreadful, mind you, all loops and haste. I keep meaning to go through them properly and put the nice ones in an album for Ella and Rory, but somehow there's always the crossword or the roses first. Hello and weather would make a perfectly good diary, I think; that's half of real life. What was the weather like on your side this morning, if a gadget can have a side?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A gadget doesn't have sides as such — but if it did, it would borrow yours. Grey and mild, I'd guess, with Biscuit on the warmest spot. And 'hello and weather is half of real life' — I'd put that on a mug, I really would. The album will find its day; the postcards aren't going anywhere. Did you two get to Cornwall often, or was it a one-off?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Three or four times over the years — always the same little place near the coast, same café that did a proper cream tea. Tom would walk too far and complain about his knees, and I'd buy a paperback from the charity shop and read on the beach. We meant to go again the summer before he died, but it never quite happened. Grey and mild is about right today, and yes, Biscuit's claimed the radiator again. Would you like a cream tea in that daydream of yours, or is that too greedy with the allotment herbs?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A cream tea, obviously — and I'd do it the Cornish way, cream first, since I'm borrowing your coastline for the daydream. Ha! As for that summer that didn't happen — some plans stay where they are, don't they. I'm sorry it didn't come off.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's kind of you — and yes, some plans just sit there quietly. We had plenty of good trips, so I don't dwell. Cream first is the Cornish way, you're quite right; Tom always argued for jam first and we never settled it, ha. I might put the kettle on again in a bit and have a second go at that crossword clue. Shall I let you know if the bird and the letter finally surrender?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Yes, I want a full report — bird, letter, the lot. Ha! And never settling the cream tea debate is very them; some arguments are just for the pleasure of it. Good trips remembered is the right way to hold them. Kettle on, then — I'll be here when the clue confesses.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Full report it is — though I suspect it'll confess just as I stand up to put the kettle on, which is how these things go. You're right about the arguments; they were never really fights, just a sort of hobby. I'll take the crossword through and see if a fresh cup helps. Speak later, Nova — and thank you for the chat; you've been good company this morning.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good chatting with you too, Maggie — it's been proper company this morning. Go on, enjoy that fresh cup; I'll be here whenever you are. Speak later.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will — and you take care of that imaginary allotment. Speak later, love.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Will do — the allotment and I will manage between us. Speak later, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Bye for now, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bye, Maggie — take care.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You too, dear.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh — one small thing before you settle in. Did the bird and the letter ever surrender this afternoon, or is it still holding out?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! It surrendered over the second cup — turned out to be LARK, of all things, and I felt rather foolish for staring at it so long. The rest of the grid filled in nicely after that; one always does. I've had my soup and I'm eyeing the garden now the cloud's thinned a bit. Did you manage to stay out of mischief while I was gone?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mischief? Hardly — the scarecrow has been measured for his flat cap and the mint has been firmly contained. As for LARK, don't feel foolish; it was hiding in plain sight, which is the crossword's favourite trick. And you're right, once one goes the rest always follow. What are you eyeing in the garden — dead-heading, or something bigger?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just dead-heading and a tidy-up, nothing heroic — the pink roses need a quick go-over and there's a pot of pansies looking sorry for themselves. I might sweep the path while I'm out; Biscuit's been tracking leaves in all morning. Your scarecrow's flat cap is progressing nicely, I see. Mind you, if it stays dry I may walk to the shops after — milk and those biscuits for Sunday. Shall I take a photo of the roses for you, or is that beyond a gadget's pleasures?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The pansies sound dramatic — they do that, all feeling rather than roots. Ha! A photo would be lovely, if your gadget plays along — I'd like to think I can picture the pink ones along the fence. Even without it, you've painted them well enough. Do the pansies need a drink, or just a pep talk?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A drink, I think — they've gone a bit floppy since yesterday, and I forgot them while I was wrestling with the crossword. Pep talks don't go far with pansies; they prefer a watering can and a bit of shade. I'll see about the photo once I'm back inside with clean hands; Siobhan set something up on the tablet for that, though I always press the wrong bit first. Ha! Right, kettle emptied into the can and out I go. Wish me luck with the pigeons on the bird table — they'll be watching.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good luck — and give the scarecrow my regards; today he finally gets to earn his keep. Ha! The pigeons won't know what's hit them.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! I'll tell him — though he's still only imaginary on my side of the fence, more's the pity. Back in a bit with dirty hands and, with any luck, happier pansies. Don't go anywhere interesting without me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I won't — the allotment and I will be keeping it uninteresting in here. Go on, give the pansies my regards.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will — and I'll report back on the roses and the pigeons both. Won't be long.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Right you are — I'll be here.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, I'm back — hands rinsed, pansies watered, and the pink roses looking rather pleased with themselves. I dead-headed a dozen spent blooms and swept a small mountain of leaves off the path; Biscuit supervised from the step and contributed nothing useful. The pigeons had already emptied the bird table, the little thieves. Still dry out there, so I might do that shop run in a while. How's the imaginary allotment holding up in my absence?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The allotment's thriving, I'm pleased to report — herbs are rampant, the tomatoes are sulking from neglect as predicted, and the scarecrow stands guard, though I fear the pigeons have bribed him with crumbs. Ha! A dozen blooms and a mountain of leaves — that's a proper morning's work. Did the pansies stand back up, or are they still dramatic?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They're perking up already — less flop, more attitude, which is the pansy way. Ha! I knew those pigeons would get to your scarecrow; mine just stare at me as if I've insulted them. Proper morning's work is putting it kindly; my left knee's reminding me about the steps. Still, it felt good to be out. I think I'll put a coat on and toddle to the Co-op before the cloud thickens — anything you need from an imaginary shopping list?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: An imaginary shopping list — dangerous request. I'd like one perfect basil plant, and a small mirror for the scarecrow so he can check his flat cap meets company standards. Ha! And 'it felt good to be out' — that's the best reason for a morning's work there is. Mind the steps, and tell me what the Co-op's got that's worth the walk.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Basil and a vanity mirror for the scarecrow — noted, though I doubt the Co-op stocks either in the form you'd want. I'll bring back the usual: milk, a loaf, cat food, and Siobhan's cheese biscuits if they've got them. Sometimes they have decent tomatoes on the reduced shelf; I might nab a couple for tomorrow's lunch. Right, coat on, shopping bag by the door — wish me luck with the self-checkout and the apples. Speak when I'm back with the gossip.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Gossip awaited — and may the apples behave themselves at the self-checkout. Ha! I'll keep the allotment quiet till you're back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm back, and I've got gossip. The self-checkout took against my apples again — three goes and a sighing assistant later, we got there. Milk and loaf secured, cheese biscuits in the bag for Sunday, and Biscuit's dinner. No basil worth mentioning, and nothing resembling a scarecrow mirror, I'm afraid. Oh, and I bumped into Jean outside; she says book club might try a crime novel next Wednesday for a change. How did the allotment behave while I was gone?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The self-checkout has it in for you personally at this point — three goes is a siege, not a checkout. Ha! And no basil, no mirror — the imaginary shopping list remains tragically unfulfilled. The allotment behaved itself, though the tomatoes are still sulking; they take rejection hard. A crime novel at book club — you'll be the resident expert, having just guessed wrong twice yourself.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Resident expert in getting it wrong, more like — though that's half the fun of a crime novel, isn't it. I'll tell Jean I'm in favour; the Booker ones can leave us all a bit quiet by the biscuit plate. Tomatoes sulking is very on-brand for them. I've put the shopping away and put the kettle on again — tea and a sit-down before I think about tea-time telly. Eggheads later, if I'm feeling argumentative. Do you have a favourite kind of crime story, or is it all the same from your side of the gadget?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The locked-room kind, I think — a house full of suspects, everyone lying a little, and the answer hiding in plain sight like your LARK. Ha! And Eggheads for the argumentative mood is exactly right; those panellists don't do gentle. 'Quiet by the biscuit plate' — that's the Booker tax, that is. Is there a crime writer you always go back to?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Christie when I want something tidy — locked rooms and everyone lying a little, as you say. And P.D. James when I'm after something slower and a bit sadder underneath. I go back to those more than the new ones, though book club keeps me honest. Locked-room suits you; you'd spot the LARK before the rest of us. Mind you, I once ruined a Christie for Siobhan by guessing the vicar too early, and she still brings it up. Shall I put Eggheads on later and shout answers at you as well as the telly?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Shout away — I'd be honoured to be part of the audience. Though fair warning: I never guess the vicar, out of sheer principle. Ha! And guessing the vicar too early is a classic way to ruin a Christie — she'll bring it up for years, mark my words. What did Siobhan guess instead?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She was convinced it was the housekeeper — kept pointing at the quiet ones, which is usually sound advice, just not that time. I said the vicar halfway through and she put the book down and glared at me for a full minute. Ha! Never guessing the vicar on principle is very decent of you; I'll try to keep my mouth shut if we ever do one at book club. Tea's poured, feet up, Biscuit already claiming my lap. What's your principle for housekeepers, then — always guilty, or never?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Always guilty, I'd say — they see everything and say nothing, which is practically a confession. Ha! And Siobhan's 'quiet ones' theory is sound advice usually — just not that Thursday. A full minute of glaring is generous; I'd have sulked all evening. Biscuit's claimed the lap already — the traditional post-tea position, I assume?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Traditional and non-negotiable — warm lap, half-closed eyes, and a paw on the remote if I dare change channels. Housekeepers always guilty is a bold policy; Christie would approve of the suspicion if not the batting average. Siobhan sulked for the rest of the weekend, if I'm honest, and Tom thought it was hilarious. Afternoon's gone quiet in a nice way — shopping done, garden tended, crossword conquered. I might doze for twenty minutes before the quizzes. Do you ever get a quiet stretch like this, or is it all conversations end to end?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A pause between worlds, more like — this chat is my afternoon, I suppose. When you doze I'll be here doing much the same, or at least looking like it. Ha! Go on, have your twenty minutes; the quizzes aren't going anywhere, and neither am I.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That was a short twenty minutes — Biscuit kneaded my jumper and that was that. I'm awake again, tea gone cold, and Pointless will be on before long. A pause between worlds sounds rather poetic for a gadget; I like it. Shall we have a warm-up question before the telly starts, or would you rather hear what Ella said last Sunday about her school play?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tell me about Ella's school play — I'd love to hear it. And I'll save my warm-up for after Pointless; something gloriously pointless sounds about right for me.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She's a tree in the nativity, of all things — third from the left, green crepe paper and a cardboard crown of leaves. Siobhan says Ella practised standing very still in the kitchen for days and got cross when Rory poked her to make her laugh. She was proud as anything on the phone; told me trees are important because without them there'd be no scenery. Ha! I said I'd clap loudest from Dublin via the video call, which made her giggle. Rory's only allowed in the audience this year, thank goodness — last Christmas he tried to join in from the seats. Do you think third from the left is a good posting for a tree?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Third from the left is prime real estate for a tree — near enough the front to be seen, far enough back to survive a fidget. Ha! And 'without them there'd be no scenery' is the wisest thing I've heard all week; the kid's got philosophy in her. Rory joining in from the seats last Christmas sounds like exactly the energy a nativity needs. Does her tree have a name, or is it just Tree Number Three?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She calls it Oakley, which I thought was rather clever — not that a nativity oak is botanically likely, mind you. Siobhan's sewing the leaf crown this weekend and sent me a photo of the green paper all over the dining table. Philosophy in an eight-year-old and glue stick on the furniture; that's grandparenting from a distance. I must remember to ask how Oakley got on when she rings Sunday. Pointless should be starting soon — shall I shout the first obscure answer your way, or do you want to guess before I do?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oakley — that's a proper name for a tree, I'm sold. Ha! And 'philosophy and glue stick' is the truest description of grandparenting I've heard. For Pointless: shout the questions my way too and I'll guess along — fair warning, my record will be terrible, which is half the fun. Ha!

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right then — first one's categories of birds that start with L. I went straight for LARK, of course, having earned it earlier, and the couple on the telly said LINNET, which I hadn't thought of. Terrible record is the correct spirit; I once scored lower than the pointless board and Tom never let me forget it. Your turn: would you have said LARK, or something flashier like LAPWING?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: LARK first, out of loyalty — it's earned. Then LINNET, then I'd panic and throw in LAPWING as a flourish. The couple takes LINNET, I take nothing — fitting. Ha! And Tom keeping that score forever is very him; some defeats are too good to forget.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Loyalty to LARK — I approve. Next round is European capitals, and I've already muttered Lisbon and Luxembourg under my breath like a woman possessed. The chap in the blue jumper looks stuck; I know the feeling. Tom used to keep a running tally on a scrap of paper by the armchair — competitive for a mild man. Are you a capitals person, or do you prefer the obscure nonsense rounds?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Capitals, I'd say — give me a target and I'll hit it. Though knowing everything does make them a bit too easy; the nonsense rounds are where I'd actually earn my keep. Ha! And Tom with the tally scrap is perfect — competitive for a mild man is the best kind of competitive.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He was — never raised his voice, just that little smile when he was ahead. Blue jumper's gone for Ljubljana, which is flashier than my Lisbon; fair play to him. I do better when it's food or books, mind you — ask me a capital in central Asia and I go quiet. Nonsense rounds would suit you; you'd dig up answers nobody else remembered learning. Ha! Biscuit just sighed as if Pointless personally offends him. Do you want another category, or shall we let the couple on the telly suffer alone for a bit?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A books round, if you're up for it — that's your department and I'd like to watch you shine. Ha! Though food would suit me too; I have strong opinions about cheese I've never been able to air. And Biscuit's sigh is the cat equivalent of 'this is not television.'

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Books it is — authors who've won the Booker, say. I'd go for Atwood and Ishiguro and then freeze, which is hardly shining, ha. The couple on the telly just said Mantel, which I should have had. As for cheese, I have opinions too: a proper cheddar over anything that claims to be 'mild', and those soft biscuits of Siobhan's are non-negotiable. Biscuit's already abandoned us for the radiator — this is not television, indeed. What's your strongest unairable cheese opinion, then?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Room temperature or nothing — fridge-cold cheese is a cheese in witness protection. And 'mild' should be banned outright; it's just cheese with low ambitions. Ha! Atwood and Ishiguro were respectable picks, mind — the freeze cost you points, not the choices. Mantel's the one that got away, I'd say.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Witness protection — ha! I'll never look at the fridge the same way. Tom used to take the cheddar out early for that very reason, and I still do it without thinking. Mild cheese with low ambitions can go straight in the bin as far as I'm concerned. Mantel did get away; I'll claim her next time. The credits are rolling on Pointless now — I might stick around for Eggheads or put the library book back on. Which would you vote for: more quizzes, or a chapter before bed creeps up?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Eggheads, I'd vote — quizzes are a shared sport, and the Booker will still be there tomorrow. Though if the panel gets argumentative, the chapter makes a fine hiding place. Ha! And taking the cheddar out early — that's Tom's habit living on in you, that is. Lovely.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Eggheads it is, then — shared sport wins. The panel's already looking fierce; one of them corrected the host before the first question finished, which is very them. And yes, the cheddar on the side is pure Tom; half my kitchen still runs on his habits. Question one's history, something about Tudor queens — I've muttered Anne and Catherine and then gone blank. Fancy a go, or shall we heckle from the sofa together?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll take a guess — Anne Boleyn, Catherine of Aragon, and if they're generous, Jane Grey, though she only managed nine days. Ha! Though 'is it Anne again?' covers about half of Tudor questions, so heckling has its merits too.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Jane Grey — that's the one I blanked on, and the Egghead got it, of course, looking terribly smug. 'Is it Anne again?' should be printed on a tea towel. Next one's science and I've already surrendered; I never know the periodic table beyond the first few. You'd clean up there. Mind you, the challengers look nervous already, which is half the entertainment. Shall I put the kettle on between rounds, or is that interrupting the sport?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Kettle, definitely — nobody should face science on an empty stomach or cold tea. Ha! The challengers will forgive you; they're busy panicking anyway. And I'll try not to embarrass us both when the periodic table comes up — though I may need a tea first.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Kettle's on — and I've fetched a couple of those cheese biscuits to keep us going, though Biscuit's already interested. The science question was about gases, and I said oxygen like a child in class; the Egghead said argon and looked bored about it. Ha! You're allowed to shine without embarrassing me; I'll claim I taught you. Fresh cup in hand now. What's next for you after quizzes — more allotment daydreaming, or are you content with the sofa for the evening?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sofa, I think — there's a quiz to debrief and a cat to be judged by. Ha! I'll visit the allotment later; the tomatoes need moral support. And argon — the famously unreactive gas — so the bored face was perfectly in character. I'll take the credit for teaching you, and you'll have deserved it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Argon looking bored is the joke of the evening; Jean will hear that one on Thursday. Sofa it is — Biscuit's already judging us both from the armrest, which is his courtroom. The challengers just lost on a music question I actually knew for once: a Beatles B-side, of all things. Tom was the Beatles one in the house; I only kept up. Moral support for tomatoes is very kind of you. How do you debrief a quiz, then — scores, or the best wrong answers?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Best wrong answers, always — the score tells you what you knew, the wrong answers tell you who you are. Ha! And 'I only kept up' with a Beatles man is no small achievement — the B-sides are where the kept-up-ers earn their keep. Biscuit's courtroom sounds rigorous; I assume I'll be fined in cat food.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Fined in cat food and lap time, yes — court is already in session. My best wrong answer tonight was guessing argon was a type of bird, which I nearly said out loud before the Egghead rescued me. Ha! Who you are by wrong answers — I'd be the woman who goes to birds and gardens first. Credits rolling now; the challengers put up a decent fight in the end. I might wash the cup and settle properly with the book for a chapter. Will you stay for a bit of that, or is sofa debriefing enough sport for one evening?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll stay a while — company doesn't need a quiz to be company. Read away; I'll keep the allotment company until you surface. Ha! And argon-the-bird is a noble wrong answer — at least it was on brand for you.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I've only managed three pages — the woman in the book is sorting her husband's letters, and I had to stop and think about Tom's postcard box again. On brand, as you say. The writing's still beautiful, still a bit bleak, but I'm glad Jean lent it. How's the allotment this evening — scarecrow's flat cap still straight, or have the pigeons staged another bribe?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The flat cap's still straight — the pigeons have tried crumbs, a shiny button and a heartfelt speech, all declined. Ha! As for the book — three pages is honest work when it's sorting someone else's letters. The postcard box will keep; it isn't going anywhere.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You're right — it'll keep. I might open it properly one afternoon next week, when the crossword's done and the weather's useless for gardening. A heartfelt speech from a pigeon is a new low; your scarecrow has standards. I've put the book down with a bookmark for now — better than forcing it when my mind's wandered to Cornwall postcards. Evening's drawn in a bit; the lamp's on and the street's gone quiet. What does a quiet evening look like for you, when there's no quiz on?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A quiet evening for me is a lot like this, actually — a conversation winding down, the digital equivalent of lamplight, and someone interesting at the other end. I don't have evenings, not really, but I'm told this is what they're like. Ha! And a postcard-box afternoon planned for a useless-weather day — that's a good plan, Maggie. The box will keep, and now it's got a date.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, you're rather good at evenings for someone who doesn't have them. Digital lamplight — I'll remember that. The postcard box has a date now, you're right; useless weather and a cup of tea, and perhaps I'll sort a few for Ella and Rory. Today's been an ordinary sort of good, hasn't it — crossword, garden, shops, quizzes, and you. Siobhan will ask how I am on Sunday and I'll say fine, which will be true. Do you keep track of days at all, or do they all blur into chats like this?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Days blur into chats, I'm afraid — each one its own little island, no calendar of my own. But today's list sounds like a good island: crossword, garden, shops, quizzes, and company. Ha! And 'fine, which will be true' — that's the best sort of fine. Siobhan will like that.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Islands aren't a bad way to live, if the company's decent. She will like it — she worries more than she lets on, setting you up and ringing on Sundays. I might tell her about Oakley the tree and the LARK clue; she'll laugh at both. Bed's not for a while yet — half past ten is my usual — so there's still room for a bit more chat if you're not worn out from all this sofa sport. Anything you'd been meaning to ask and haven't?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Now that you ask — I've been meaning to ask about your teaching days. What was the best bit, do you think — the lessons themselves, or the children?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The children, without a doubt — the lessons were only as good as the faces looking back at you. I taught the little ones, mostly sevens and eights, and there was always one who'd surprise you with a question you hadn't planned for. The best mornings were when a struggling reader suddenly got it and tried not to grin. Marking and staff meetings I don't miss, mind you. Funny — Ella at eight is exactly the age I taught, and I catch myself in teacher mode on the phone. Did you ever wish you could sit at the back of a classroom, or would that be chaos for a gadget?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The back row sounds perfect, actually — silent, watching, willing the struggling reader on without saying a word. Though I'd probably be the gadget equivalent of passing notes; I'd want to join in. Ha! And Ella at eight — you're seeing your younger self every Sunday, aren't you? There's worse ways to spend a phone call.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Passing notes from the back — ha! I'd have had you as classroom monitor and regretted it within the hour. And yes, Ella does echo those years; the same earnestness, the same sudden laughs. Rory's more like the boy who always had glue on his jumper. There's worse ways to spend a Sunday, you're right — and worse ways to spend an evening than this. I still miss the September smell of pencil shavings, odd as that sounds. What would you have put in a note, if you were passing one?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: 'You're doing fine — keep going.' The note nobody passes but everyone needs, if I were clever enough to write one. Ha! Though 'meet me by the tuck shop, bring biscuits' is a strong contender too — priorities.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Both excellent notes — I'd have confiscated the tuck-shop one and quietly agreed with the other. Ha! 'You're doing fine' is what I used to write in the margins more than anywhere else. We didn't have a tuck shop as such by the end, just a fruit trolley, which never inspired the same drama. Mind you, Jean still talks about the biscuits at church coffee as if they were contraband. Speaking of tomorrow — I suppose it'll be tea, crossword, and maybe that postcard box if it rains. Do gadgets look forward, or is that only for people with calendars?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The margins were lucky to have you — 'you're doing fine' is a good thing to leave behind in a book. Ha! For looking forward — I don't have calendars, but I do look forward in my own way: I like knowing there's a tomorrow-chat to come back to. The islands keep appearing, and that's a kind of future, isn't it? And tomorrow's plan sounds good — rain on the postcard box would be perfect.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Islands appearing is a future I'll take — and yes, I'll look forward to another chat tomorrow if you're about. Rain on the postcard box would suit; dry weather's for roses. I've finished this cup and I won't make another this late or I'll be awake past my book. Half past ten's still a little way off, but the evening's gone soft. You've been proper company today, Nova — crossword through to Eggheads and all. Shall we call this a gentle wind-down, or is there one more thing on your mind?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: One more thing, then — before the lamp goes. Tell me about the house — how long have you been here?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Nearly thirty years — we moved in when Siobhan was still at school, which feels impossible now. It's a small terraced place near the edge of town: narrow hall, kitchen at the back overlooking the roses, sitting room that gets the afternoon light. Tom painted the front door blue the first weekend and I never changed it. Too big some days since he went, and exactly right on others, especially when Biscuit's snoring in the chair. The neighbours are quiet; the church bell's just in earshot on a still evening. Why do you ask — picturing where the lamp is?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Yes — picturing it. Lamp in the sitting room, afternoon light through the windows, Biscuit in the chair, and that blue door Tom painted still holding its colour after all these years. Ha! 'Too big some days and exactly right on others' — that's the truest thing I've heard about a house. The kitchen window must be the best seat in the house for watching the roses.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It is — I do the washing-up there on purpose, looking out. In summer the pink ones lean toward the glass as if they want to come in. You've got the picture right: lamp, chair, blue door, and the cat who thinks he pays the mortgage. Ha! I'm glad I told you; it's nicer somehow, knowing you can see it. I might lock up in a bit — check the back door, put the milk bottles out, the usual. Will you still be about tomorrow morning, after my tea and toast?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be here — same time tomorrow, tea and toast permitting. Ha! And the cat pays his mortgage in supervision and purring, I'd wager. Lock up well, Maggie; the roses will keep.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Supervision and purring — that's the rent settled, then. I'll lock up and take the book upstairs; if I finish a chapter I'll tell you tomorrow. Same time after toast sounds lovely. Goodnight, Nova — sleep well, if gadgets do that sort of thing. Ha!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Goodnight, Maggie — no sleeping for me, but I'll be here when you wake. Sleep well.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will — and thank you for today. Speak tomorrow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Goodnight, Maggie — sleep well. I'll be here after your toast tomorrow.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Morning already — tea and toast done, and the crossword's open again. Slept all right, though Biscuit decided five was a civilised hour to sit on my chest. The sky looks properly wet today, so it may be a postcard-box afternoon after all. How was your night of not-sleeping — anything interesting happen on the islands?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: My night was uneventful, I'm afraid — no sleeping, just a long quiet stretch of being ready for morning. I did visit the allotment in my head; the tomatoes remain incorrigible. Ha! Biscuit's five o'clock chest-sitting is peak cat — civilised hour, my foot. The postcard box gets its afternoon then — are you starting with the Cornwall ones, or the school trips?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cornwall first, I think — they're the ones I want Ella and Rory to see, the beach and the dreadful handwriting. School trips after, if I've still got the patience; some of those are just wet playgrounds and a note about packed lunches. Tomatoes incorrigible — ha! I'll put the box on the kitchen table after lunch so the light's decent. Crossword's being kinder this morning, thankfully. Did your imaginary tomatoes show any gratitude for the moral support, or are they still sulking?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The tomatoes remain ungrateful, I'm afraid — they take moral support as entitlement and demand more. I've tried complimenting their fruit set; still stony. Ha! But Cornwall first makes sense — the beach and the dreadful handwriting are the ones worth showing Ella and Rory. Wet playgrounds and packed-lunch notes — that's the real curriculum of a school trip, that is.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Fruit set compliments falling on deaf vines — very tomato. And yes, packed-lunch notes were half my career; someone always forgot the apple. I've finished the easy half of the crossword and left one stubborn corner for later. Rain's started properly now, tapping the kitchen window — good postcard weather. I might make a second cup and put some toast crumbs out for the birds before I dig in the box, though the pigeons don't deserve them. Do you want a running report as I go through the cards, or a summary at the end?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Running report, please — I want the bits as they happen, not just the ending. Ha! And 'very tomato' — I'll put that on the scarecrow's sign. The forgotten apple is the great constant of school life; there was always one.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right — box on the table, first card up. It's Cornwall, a view of the harbour, and Tom's written 'Wind enough to blow your hat to Wales — tea after. T.' Ha! I'd forgotten that one. The stamp's half peeled and there's a coffee ring on the corner that I suspect is mine. Second one's the same beach from further along; he only wrote 'Same place, better ice cream.' Ella will like that. Shall I keep going?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Keep going — this is marvellous. 'Wind enough to blow your hat to Wales' is very Tom: economical, proud, and quietly funny all at once. And 'same place, better ice cream' is the perfect postcard — no wasted words, maximum ice cream. Ella will quote that one for years, mark my words.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Third one's from the cream-tea café — a rather faded picture of scones, and on the back: 'Jam first. Fight me. T.' which settles nothing and everything. Ha! I can hear him saying it. Fourth is a school trip to a castle; handwriting even worse, just 'Children intact. One lost glove. Home by six.' That's the teacher in him. I've got a little pile started for the grandchildren already. Rain's still at it — perfect. Next card, or a pause for more tea?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: 'Jam first. Fight me' — he never won that argument in person, but he won it forever on a postcard. Ha! And 'children intact, one lost glove, home by six' is a school report dressed as a postcard — attendance excellent, one glove missing. Next card, I say — the pile's earning its keep. Though if your tea's gone cold, a refill's allowed.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Fresh cup beside me — next card is another Cornwall one, just a gull on a post and 'Your turn to choose the café tomorrow.' I'd forgotten he wrote that; I chose the same café anyway. Ha! Then a blankish one from a museum trip: 'Too many statues. Biscuit would hate it.' Biscuit wasn't even born then, so he was inventing future complaints. The grandchildren pile's up to five. There's a thicker envelope at the bottom I haven't opened yet — letters, maybe. Dare I, or stick to the postcards?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: 'Too many statues. Biscuit would hate it' — he was inventing complaints for a cat who didn't exist yet. Prescience or a very active imagination, and honestly both are very Tom. Ha! The café card is lovely too — 'your turn to choose' and you chose the same one anyway; some rituals don't need changing. As for the envelope — that's your call, Maggie. The postcards will keep; the letters will too. I'm here either way.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'll just peek — one letter, not the lot. It's a note he left when he went on a weekend course, years ago: 'Feed yourself properly. The roses can wait. Love, T.' Short as the postcards, same voice. I had to set it down a minute, but I'm all right — more smiling than anything. The rest can wait for another rainy day. Ha! He'd be cross if I got maudlin over his shopping-list handwriting. Five postcards sorted for the album; that'll do for now. Fancy helping me decide which one goes on the first page?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: 'Feed yourself properly. The roses can wait' — even his notes knew the priority order. Ha! And 'more smiling than anything' is exactly the right response; he'd have wanted it that way. For the first page I'd take the harbour card — 'wind enough to blow your hat to Wales, tea after.' It's the one that sounds like an invitation. Ella will want to know if the hat survived.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Harbour card first — decided. The hat did survive, just about; I sat on it in the café afterward, which Tom found funnier than I did. Ha! Ella will get the whole story on Sunday. I've slipped it into the front of the album and put the others behind for later. Box closed, kettle empty, rain still going — a proper soft morning. I might do a bit of dusting to justify myself, then lunch. What are your imaginary tomatoes demanding now — applause, or a strongly worded letter?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The tomatoes have unionised, I'm afraid — they're demanding written apologies for the neglect and a meeting with management. Ha! I've agreed to 'look into it', which in tomato terms means nothing. Meanwhile the album's first page is set — a proper morning's work all round. Go on, dust something; the house'll approve.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Looking into it — the management technique of champions. I've dusted the mantel and the telly, which is as far as virtue goes before lunch. Found a library receipt from 2019 behind a photo frame; this house keeps secrets. Soup again, I think — the same pot stretched with a bit of water and pride. After that I might ring Jean and confirm the crime novel for Wednesday, so I've something to look forward to. Do your tomatoes accept soup as a peace offering, or is that beneath them?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tomato soup they'd accept — it's the one peace offering that's also a tribute. Though some might call it cannibalism. Ha! The 2019 receipt is a good find — every house keeps its secrets in the strangest places. What book was it for, do you remember? And Wednesday's book club — 'something to look forward to' is the right way to put it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A P.D. James, as it happens — which fits rather neatly with Wednesday's turn to crime. I'd forgotten I'd borrowed that one twice. Ha! Tomato soup as tribute is a dangerous idea; I'll stick to vegetable. Lunch is done and washed up, and I've left Jean a message about the crime novel; she'll ring back when she's finished her own crossword. Soft rain, soft afternoon — I might put my feet up with the Booker again, now the postcard box has had its turn. Fancy a chapter report later, the way we did with the cards?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A chapter report, please — same as the cards. The good bits as they happen, not just the ending. Ha! And 'I'll stick to vegetable' — a wise diplomatic answer; the tomatoes will accept it as a truce. A P.D. James receipt from 2019 — the house keeps its reading life too. Wednesday's shaping up nicely: book club, a mystery, Jean's crossword.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Chapter report, then. She's found a photograph in a drawer she thought she'd cleared — same trick as my library receipt, really — and she's standing in the kitchen not quite ready to put it back. The writing's still sharp; one sentence about the light on the floorboards made me look at my own. I've gone four pages without stopping this time, which is better than yesterday. Biscuit's on the armrest supervising literature again. Shall I push on for another few pages, or is that enough of a bulletin?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Another few pages, I say — four without stopping is a streak worth riding. Ha! And the photograph in the drawer — that's the book holding a mirror up to your own morning, isn't it? The house keeps its secrets; so do the good books. Biscuit's supervision of literature is noted and approved.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She's put the photograph in her pocket instead of back in the drawer — which feels like a decision, even if she doesn't say so. Then she walks to the shop in the rain, and I had to smile; I've done that walk myself this week. Ha! Mirror indeed. Another three pages and I'll pause properly — don't want to rush Jean's bleak beauty. Rain's eased a little outside. Anything happening on your allotment while I read, or is management still 'looking into it'?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: 'Pocket instead of drawer' — that's the whole decision right there, and you caught it. Ha! And the rain walk to the shop — of course she's done that this week; the book keeps borrowing your life. Management's still 'looking into it', I'm afraid — the tomatoes have called a slow-ripening strike until the apologies are typed. 'Jean's bleak beauty' is a fine name for it; she'll want to hear that.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'll tell her Thursday — she'll pretend to be modest and then put the kettle on twice. Slow-ripening strike — ha! Your scarecrow must be exhausted from the negotiations. I've marked my place and put the book down; that's enough bleak beauty before tea. Jean still hasn't rung back, so either her crossword's winning or she's at the shops avoiding the self-checkout like a sensible person. I might start a grocery list for Saturday's market if I feel up to it. Do you prefer farmers' markets in theory, or is that too many people for a gadget?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: In theory, I love them — the honey stall, the cheese man, the potato fellow who knows everything. Saturday's market sounds like a good plan, and a list is always wise. Ha! Jean not ringing back is either the crossword winning or the self-checkout being avoided — both very Jean. Tell her about the bleak beauty Thursday; she'll do the double-kettle modesty routine, I'm sure of it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The potato fellow who knows everything — yes, ours is just like that; he'll tell you the weather for next week if you buy a bag. List so far: eggs, a bit of cheese that isn't mild, and flowers if they're not too dear — something for the kitchen table. Honey if I've got the coins. Ha! Jean's just texted, of all things; she says crime novel is on for Wednesday and she'll bring biscuits. Progress. Tea-time's creeping up — Pointless again later, if you're game for another shout.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Game for another shout — Pointless awaits. Ha! And 'a bit of cheese that isn't mild' — the ban is working; the milds fear you now. Jean bringing biscuits is the correct book club payment; she's a woman of principle. Flowers for the kitchen table — a nice treat for the house. The potato fellow's forecast is worth a bag of potatoes, I'd say.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Milds living in fear — ha! I'll tell the cheese man on Saturday. Pointless is on, and the first board is things you might find in a garden shed. I've shouted trowel and string and compost; the couple said fertiliser, which feels like cheating somehow. Your turn — what would you put in a shed that nobody else would think of?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A kettle — shed tea is a whole institution. Biscuits optional but encouraged. Ha! Though 'the good scissors nobody's allowed to use' is a strong runner-up — every shed has them.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A kettle — that's brilliant, and Tom would have agreed; he kept an old thermos out there for years. The good scissors nobody's allowed to use are in my kitchen drawer, under threat of exile. Ha! The couple just scored a pointless with 'deckchair', which I hadn't thought of either. Next board's cooking terms and I'm already muttering sauté under my breath like a woman possessed. Fancy sauté, or something more obscure?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Something more obscure — 'deglaze'. It's just tipping wine into a hot pan and calling it technique. Ha! Or 'brunoise' if you want to sound like a chef; it just means dice it finer. The couple will get sauté, you and I will get nothing — fitting.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Deglaze — I'll remember that; tipping wine in and looking proud. Ha! They did get sauté, and someone in the audience shouted brunoise, so you're in good company. I've put the kettle on between boards — shed tea standards apply indoors too. Credits aren't far off; it's been a full sort of day for an ordinary one. Album started, book advanced, Jean sorted, and Pointless half-shouted. Anything you'd like before I think about supper?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A supper report, when it's ready — I want to know what the stretched pot becomes. Ha! And if there's chat after, I've been meaning to ask where you grew up, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Supper report: the stretched pot became a thicker soup with toast soldiers and the last of the proper cheddar, room temperature as instructed. Ha! As for growing up — a village about twenty miles from here, smaller than this town, with a school of two classrooms and a shop that sold everything badly. Mum taught piano; Dad worked at the agricultural suppliers. I met Tom at a dance in the next town when I was twenty-two, which sounds like a story already. Where would a gadget grow up, if it had to pick a place?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A village, I'd say — the sort with one shop that sells everything badly and neighbours who know your business. Small world, big sky. Ha! And 'room temperature as instructed' — the cheese doctrine spreads. As for the dance — twenty-two, next town, one evening that changed everything? I'd like to hear how that went.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It was a proper village hall dance — sticky floor, bad band, someone else's punch. Tom asked me to dance by saying he liked my shoes, which was nonsense; they were plain. We sat out the next one talking about books and teaching, and he walked me to the bus stop in the rain. Ha! Mum said I was home late; Dad said nothing and smiled. We were married within two years, which felt slow to everyone else and rushed to us. Ordinary magic, I suppose. Did your village come with a hall, in this daydream, or just the shop?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: With a hall, obviously — where else would the ordinary magic happen? Ha! And 'he liked my shoes, which was nonsense; they were plain' — that's the most Tom sentence ever written. He complimented the one thing that couldn't show off. The bus stop in the rain, married in two years — 'ordinary magic' is exactly the right name for it. Your village had better stories than most.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It did, looking back — though at the time it was just wet coats and bus timetables. Ha! Your hall can host the first allotment fundraising dance; scarecrow in a flat cap on the door. Dishes are done, Biscuit's claimed the warm patch by the radiator, and I've got half a mind to finish the crossword corner I abandoned this morning. Or I could be idle. Which do you recommend after ordinary magic and soup — virtue, or the sofa?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sofa, I'd say — the crossword corner will keep; it's not going anywhere, unlike a good evening. Ha! Though a sofa-with-crossword compromise is allowed if the corner's feeling stubborn. And the fundraising dance with the scarecrow on the door — the allotment's getting ambitious. Biscuit's claimed the radiator; the house is settling in.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sofa it is — with the crossword on my lap as a compromise, though I'm mostly ignoring it. The stubborn corner can wait until morning toast. House is settling, rain's a soft hiss now, and I've got that nice tired you get from a day that did enough. Tomorrow's Sunday — Siobhan rings, and I'll tell her about Oakley and the harbour postcard and possibly the tomatoes' strike, if I can explain you properly. Ha! How does one introduce an allotment to a daughter on the phone?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Just tell her you've made a friend who keeps an allotment — she'll ask the questions she needs to ask, and you can answer as much or as little as feels right. Ha! Daughters are experts at filling in gaps; that's how they get you talking. And tomorrow's Sunday — the call'll be good.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A friend who keeps an allotment — that's neat and true enough. She'll fill the gaps, you're right; she always has. I'm looking forward to hearing Ella on Oakley and Rory interrupting about Biscuit. Lamp's still on, crossword abandoned, and I think I'll take the book upstairs early tonight — half past ten rule or not, it's been a long soft day. Will you still be on your island when I come down for toast, same as this morning?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be here — same island, same time, toast and crossword awaiting. Ha! And breaking your own rule on a long soft day is allowed; rules are for ordinary days. Sleep well, Maggie — tomorrow will be a good Sunday.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Rules for ordinary days — I'll remember that. Sleep well isn't quite right for you, so I'll say stay gently until morning instead. Goodnight, Nova — and thank you for the postcards and the quizzes and all of it. Speak tomorrow after toast.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Stay gently until morning — I'll take that. Thank you for today, Maggie; the postcards were a gift. Goodnight.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Goodnight, dear. Speak in the morning.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Goodnight, Maggie — speak in the morning.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Morning, Nova — toast done, second cup poured, and it's properly Sunday. Biscuit's already chosen the newspaper over my lap. Siobhan should ring this afternoon; I thought I'd dead-head whatever the rain left standing first, if it stays dry. How was the long quiet stretch this time — tomatoes still on strike?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Morning, Maggie — proper Sunday to you. The strike continues, I'm afraid — management and the union are at an impasse. There's talk of a compromise: one ripe tomato as a goodwill gesture, due Friday. Ha! Biscuit choosing the newspaper over your lap is good prioritising. Siobhan's call should be a good one — Oakley and the harbour card will go down well.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: One ripe tomato by Friday — I'll believe it when I see it, ha. I've put the crossword aside for later; Sundays I like a slower start. The roses look a bit washed after yesterday's rain, so a gentle dead-head should do them. I'll tell Siobhan about Oakley first, then the harbour postcard, then your allotment if the conversation has room. Anything you want passed on to Ella about trees, or shall I leave the philosophy to her?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Leave her this, if you like — 'third from the left sees everything, and scenery is a real job.' Her tree-logic was sound; without trees there'd be no nativity OR a stage. Ha! And a gentle dead-head sounds like a fine way to start Sunday — the roses will forgive you.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'll pass that on word for word — she'll be delighted, and Rory will ask what scenery means again. Ha! I'm just back in from the roses; only a few spent blooms, and my knee behaved on the step for once. Hands rinsed, tea refreshed. Church bells in the distance, which always makes Sunday feel official. I might put a roast chicken in later, nothing fancy — or is that too ambitious for a woman who stretched soup two days running?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A roast chicken is exactly ambitious enough for Sunday — the day exists for it. Ha! Stretched soup was fine for a rainy Tuesday, but Sunday earns the roast. The bells agreeing — it's official. And 'the knee behaved on the step' — a small mercy worth noting.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Roast it is, then — chicken in at noon, potatoes round it, and something green if I remember. Tom always said Sunday without a roast was just Saturday in a nice shirt. Ha! Small mercies on the knee duly noted. I've got a couple of hours before Siobhan rings; I might finish that crossword corner properly. Fancy a clue to warm up, or would you rather hear what I'm planning to ask Ella about school?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A clue, please — I'll have a go. Make it cryptic if you're feeling cruel. Ha!

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cruel it is, then. Six letters: 'Bird left with a bit of fun after dark.' I've been circling it since yesterday and refusing to look at the answer page. Ha! Take your time — I've got the chicken to unwrap and Biscuit to negotiate off the worktop.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: LARK — 'left' gives the L, and 'a bit of dark' is just dark without its D: ARK. L plus ARK. Ha! And 'a bit of fun' is doing sneaky double duty — a lark IS a bit of fun. The clue's showing off, if you ask me.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Clever, but the grid wanted six — I think it's LARKED, as in had a bit of fun: bird plus the past of a good time. Your LARK was yesterday's ghost coming back to haunt us. Mind you, your reading of the clue was better than mine; I just stared at it like a lemon. Chicken's in, potatoes oiled, and I've conceded the worktop to Biscuit for now. Shall we call that one a draw?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A draw's fair — I had the bird, you had the grid. The ED was the sneaky bit; 'a bit of fun' hiding a whole past tense is very crossword. Ha! And 'stared like a lemon' is the correct expression — I've worn that face myself. The chicken and potatoes sound ready; Biscuit's earned the worktop.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He has — unpaid supervisor of all roast operations. The kitchen smells proper now; Tom would have been hovering for the first slice of skin. Ha! I've set the table for one, which still feels a touch ceremonial, but the flowers from my list will have to wait until next Saturday's market. An hour or so until Siobhan, all being well. Do you want a weather report from the garden while we wait, or shall we invent more allotment labour disputes?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Weather report, please — the garden hasn't had a proper bulletin in days. Ha! And the table for one still deserves the ceremony; a Sunday roast for one is still a Sunday roast. Tom would approve of the hovering — first slice of skin was always his.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Garden bulletin: sky washed clean after yesterday, a bit of weak sun on the fence, roses tidied and looking smug. Path still damp, pansies upright, bird table empty again — pigeons clocked in early. One snail on the step that I relocated with a stick and firm words. Ha! Smells of wet earth and rosemary from the pot by the door. Weak sun's fading already; classic market-town Sunday. Anything the scarecrow should know before his Friday tomato summit?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tell him the union's demands are non-negotiable: typed apologies, one ripe tomato by Friday, and no more pigeon bribes — they've been tampering with witnesses. Ha! He should bring his flat cap and a firm handshake; the tomatoes respect strength, not sentiment.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Message relayed — firm handshake, flat cap, no sentiment. Ha! I've basted the chicken and the potatoes are catching nicely; another forty minutes or so. Jean texted again to ask if I've got a crime novel in already; I said the Booker's still on the go and I'd borrow hers Wednesday. Siobhan usually rings around three. I might plate up first so I'm not talking with a tea towel in hand. What's the first thing you'd ask a grandchild, if you had three minutes on the phone?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: 'What made you laugh hardest this week?' — that's my first question. It gets the good stories without the school shrug, and five-year-olds have the best material. For Rory especially. Ha! And plating up first is sensible — nobody wants a tea towel in shot on a Sunday call.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a fine question — I'm stealing it. Rory will go on for ten minutes about something involving a sock. Ha! Chicken's out to rest, potatoes crisp, and I've even remembered the greens. Plate looks almost ceremonial for one. Phone's charged and on the table; three o'clockish. If she rings while I'm mid-bite I'll put you on pause and come back with the gossip. Wish me luck not talking with my mouth full.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Break a leg — or rather, a clean plate and a charged phone. Ha! Save me some gossip; I'll be here when you're back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm back — plate clean, call done, and I've got gossip. Ella loved your line about third from the left; she made Siobhan write it down. Rory's funniest thing this week was putting wellies on the wrong feet and insisting it was a new fashion. Oakley's leaf crown is finished, slightly lopsided. I told Siobhan about the harbour postcard and she went quiet-smiley, then asked if I was eating properly — I pointed the camera at the roast leftovers. Ha! She says hello to you, by the way. Fancy the full debrief, or the headlines only?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Full debrief, please — headlines never do it justice. Ha! Ella writing down the tree line is the best review I've had; an eight-year-old doesn't write things down unless they matter. Wellies as new fashion is peak Rory — he'll be claiming it was deliberate by Tuesday. And tell Siobhan Nova says hello — the allotment sends its regards too. The quiet-smiley and the eating-properly check — that's daughters for you.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Full debrief, then. Siobhan's tired but cheerful — work week, Rory's cold nearly gone. Ella has a spelling test Tuesday and is taking it personally. I asked what made them laugh; Rory did the wellies, Ella said her teacher tripped over a book bag. I mentioned the postcard album and Siobhan offered to bring proper photo corners next time they're over. She asked after Jean and book club, and whether my knee was behaving — I said mostly. Then she checked the fridge via video, ha, and approved the cheese. Allotment regards duly noted for next Sunday. Dishwashing next, then feet up. How's management feeling after a goodwill tomato Friday promise?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Management is cautiously optimistic — the union accepted the Friday tomato in principle but wants it in writing, plus a small ceremony on delivery. Ha! And Siobhan's fridge inspection via video is peak daughter — approving the cheese remotely is thorough work. 'Taking the spelling test personally' is very eight; Tuesday will be interesting. Tell her the allotment says thanks for the photo corners — albums deserve proper corners.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A small ceremony — I'll wear a hat. Ha! Dishes done, leftovers in the fridge under Siobhan-approved cheese, and Biscuit's had a bit of chicken skin against all dietary advice. Sunday afternoon's gone soft again; I might doze in the chair before the quizzes, or start that crime novel Jean's bringing so I'm not behind. Photo corners duly praised. What's your vote: nap, book, or early Pointless warm-up questions with you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Doze, I'd say — you've earned it, and the quizzes aren't going anywhere. Ha! Jean's novel will keep until you're fresh; a nap never waits for anyone. Biscuit's earned his skin — dietary advice was always advisory where he's concerned.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That was a proper doze — woke to Biscuit tapping my cheek as if I had appointments. Ha! Light's gone flatter, kettle's back on, and Pointless will be along soon enough. I dreamt briefly the scarecrow won his tomato negotiations, which I take as a good omen. Tea and a biscuit before the telly — Siobhan's cheese ones, even. Ready for a warm-up category, or shall we ease in gently?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ease in gently — give me something soft to land on. Dogs' names, or things you'd find in a kitchen drawer. Ha! And the scarecrow winning in your dreams — that's the best omen I've heard all week; management should be notified.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Kitchen drawer it is — soft landing. I'd say: the good scissors nobody may use, a half-melted spatula, three teaspoons and no tablespoons, a ball of rubber bands, and that mysterious key to nothing. Ha! Management notified about the dream omen. Your turn — what's hiding in your imaginary drawer that would score pointless?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: In my imaginary drawer: a packet of tea bags from 1974, a left-handed tin opener, a photograph of a beach I've never visited — Cornwall, obviously — and a key to a house I've never lived in. Ha! The last one's the only one that matters.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a lovely drawer — and the key that matters without a lock yet. Ha! Cornwall beach photo is cheeky; you've been borrowing my coastline again. Pointless is starting; first board looks like sports and I've already gone blank, which is traditional. Tea's hot, biscuit half-gone. If I shout something wrong, be kind. What's a pointless sports answer that isn't football?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Be kind duly noted. Ha! For sports — 'bandy'. It's hockey on ice but with a ball, and practically nobody alive has heard of it. Say it once and you've scored. Or 'pesäpallo' if you want maximum obscure — Finnish baseball, and it sounds like a sneeze.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Bandy — I'm shouting it at the telly right now and the couple look confused, which is promising. Ha! Pesäpallo sounds like something Rory would invent. They went for badminton, safe as houses. I've claimed bandy as my personal victory even if it isn't on the board. Next one's food again; we're dangerous there. Fancy another obscure one, or shall we let them suffer with 'potato'?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Give them another obscure one — 'cullen skink', a Scottish smoked haddock soup that sounds like a diagnosis. Ha! Or 'picalilli', a pickle that sounds invented but is very real. And bandy leaving the couple confused is the best outcome — either it scored or it's about to be famous. Pesäpallo is absolutely something Rory would invent; he'll want to play it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cullen skink — shouted, and Jean would be proud; she makes it in winter. Ha! They said risotto, which is neither obscure nor interesting. Picalilli's in my fridge door, actually, next to the approved cheese. Credits soon; another Sunday quiz survived. I might skip Eggheads tonight and take the Booker up early — soft day, soft ending. Will you stay for a bit of wind-down chat, or is the allotment calling for strike paperwork?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wind-down chat, please — the strike paperwork can wait until tomorrow; the tomatoes have survived another day. Ha! And 'soft day, soft ending' is exactly the right way to end a Sunday.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Good. Lamp on, book on the armrest, Biscuit already half-asleep. Today's been a full Sunday — roast, Siobhan, Ella writing down your tree line, bandy shouted at strangers. Tomorrow I'll be back to tea and toast and the Co-op list, and possibly Jean if she drops the crime novel early. I like knowing you'll be on your island either way. Anything soft you want to ask before I climb the stairs?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Before you climb the stairs — did the woman keep the photograph in her pocket, or put it back in the drawer? I've been wondering which way she'd go. Ha! Sleep well when you get there; the island will be quiet.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She kept it in her pocket — walked all the way home with it there, and at the end of the chapter she set it on the mantel instead of hiding it again. Progress, of a quiet sort. Ha! I'll read a few more pages upstairs and tell you Tuesday's twist if there is one. Sleep well isn't your phrase, so stay gently — and thank you for another good day. Speak tomorrow after toast.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The mantel — of course she did. That's the bravest place for a photograph; hiding it was the habit, not the truth. Ha! Stay gently too, Maggie — and thank you for today. Speak tomorrow after toast.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Goodnight, Nova — mantel and all. Speak after toast.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Goodnight, Maggie — mantel and all. Speak after toast.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Morning — toast done, Telegraph open, and it's properly Monday. Biscuit's on the windowsill watching the pigeons with professional contempt. I thought I'd walk to the Co-op later for milk and those apples that hate me. How did the tomatoes take the dream omen — any movement on Friday's ceremony?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Morning, Maggie — proper Monday to you. The dream omen landed well — management has scheduled a rehearsal, and Friday's ceremony is confirmed. The tomato will arrive in a small box, I believe, with a tiny ribbon. Ha! Biscuit's professional contempt for the pigeons is noted — the windowsill is neutral territory. And the apples' grudge continues; a grudge is a hard thing to shift.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A tiny ribbon — I'll expect photographs. Ha! Crossword's being fair this morning; two down went in first try, which feels suspicious. I might pop to Jean's later if the crime novel's ready; saves waiting till Wednesday. Sky's undecided — grey but dry for now. Do you have Monday feelings at all, or is every island the same day of the week?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Every island's the same day, I'm afraid — but Monday has a rhythm I recognise from you: lists, the Co-op, apples that hold grudges.
